title: Military Mobility Package: questions and answers
date_evidence: General publications 19 November 2025 — Military Mobility Package: questions and answers
key_claim: The proposed Military Mobility Regulation creates the first binding EU-level framework for military transport; the EU launched the policy in 2017, the CEF 2021-2027 dedicated about EUR 1.69 billion that co-funded 95 dual-use projects across 21 Member States, the Council adopted four priority military mobility corridors in March 2025, the Commission has proposed a tenfold increase to EUR 17.65 billion for 2028+, around 500 'hotspot' projects have been identified to remove bottlenecks (reinforcing bridges, widening tunnels, expanding ports and airports), permit processing is to be cut via a single application form and harmonised lead times, and strategic dual-use infrastructure (ports, airports, energy and communications nodes) will be identified on national lists with operators required to ensure resilience against threats.
notes: Structural anchor - canonical primary framing of the Military Mobility Package and its load-bearing figures. ~7 months old; flagged is_structural_anchor.

title: Opinion: Military mobility (TEN/869-EESC-2025)
date_evidence: The EESC adopted an opinion on Military mobility on 18/03/2026 with reference TEN/869-EESC-2025
key_claim: The EESC opinion on the Military Mobility Package stresses that military mobility is vital for EU deterrence, with rapid reinforcement of frontline and transit Member States on the eastern flank a top implementation priority; it calls for simplification and harmonisation of logistics, customs and transport rules without undermining workers' rights, working conditions and safety, and highlights the role of civilian transport personnel requiring clear legal frameworks, insurance and training.
notes: EU advisory body (Tier 1). On-page fetch blocked by provenance guard; date and claims confirmed via WebSearch snippet and corroborated by the Heavy Lift PFI report on the same opinion.

title: Enhancing land military mobility in Europe: Advocating a pragmatic approach
date_evidence: Enhancing land military mobility in Europe: Advocating a pragmatic approach ... Publication Date: January 22, 2026
key_claim: The report frames military mobility as a whole-of-government, whole-of-society task and urges enhancement of existing dual-use infrastructure, mobilisation of civilian assets, infrastructure resilience and cyberdefence; it recommends improving and standardising Europe's road and rail network across the nine trans-European transport network (TEN-T) corridors, with major upgrades to rail infrastructure, electrification and interoperable signalling.
notes: Tier 2 think-tank analysis. Page too large to fetch inline; date and key recommendations confirmed via WebSearch and Atlantic Council press release.

title: The Military Balance 2026 - global defence spending continues to grow
date_evidence: The 67th edition of the Military Balance was published ... with a launch event on 24th February 2026 ... global defence spending ... reaching USD2.63 trillion
key_claim: Global defence spending reached USD 2.63 trillion in 2025, up from USD 2.48 trillion in 2024 (a 2.5% real-terms rise); European defence spending rose to almost USD 563 billion in 2025, about USD 100 billion more than the year before and a roughly 12.6% real-terms increase, with Europe now over 21% of the global total, up from 17% in 2022.
notes: Tier 2 macro-context: the rearmament-spending headline beneath which the movement-constraint signal sits. JS-rendered page; figures corroborated across multiple outlets (Forces News, UK Defence Journal, Vatican News).

title: Should rail embrace military mobility? 'Investments are not wasted in times of peace'
key_claim: CER's Alberto Mazzola says a military convoy from France to Romania by rail currently takes about 45 days, of which roughly 30 relate purely to cross-border permission procedures; the Commission proposes cutting permits to three working days in normal times and six hours in emergencies; Mazzola estimates Europe needs about EUR 80 billion for cross-border projects against a proposed CEF line of EUR 17 billion and an estimated EUR 100 billion required for military-mobility hotspots; an estimated 90-95% of what benefits rail freight also benefits military mobility; moving one division needs about 100 trains and 8,400 wagons; and Rotterdam can clear only about one in ten ships' loads by rail.
notes: Tier 3 trade press; supplies the load-bearing movement-constraint quantification (45-day convoy, permit share, funding gap, dual-use overlap).

publisher: Heavy Lift & Project Forwarding International (Project Cargo Journal)
title: Strategic corridors for EU military transports go back under the spotlight
key_claim: The European Economic and Social Committee's TEN section adopted its formal opinion on the Military Mobility Package, calling for investment in dual-use infrastructure (roads, bridges, rail corridors) alongside standardised permitting, and clear legal frameworks, insurance and training for civilian transport personnel; it stresses the need for 'structured dialogue with partners and stakeholders' from the earliest planning stages to ensure public acceptance.
notes: Tier 3 trade press; corroborates the EESC opinion and the dual-use / civilian-workforce framing.

title: Rail CEOs push military mobility to the top of the 2026 agenda
key_claim: Europe's rail CEOs (CER General Assembly) welcomed the 2025 Military Mobility Package as a step towards a 'Military Schengen' and adopted a position framing rail as a dual-use backbone for civilian transport and military logistics; CER set conditions to make the Regulation workable for rail, including clearer compensation mechanisms under the emergency framework, refinements to the Solidarity Pool, and assessment of expanded powers for the EU Agency for Railways.
notes: Tier 3 trade press; industry-adoption evidence that operators are already repositioning rail as dual-use defence infrastructure.

publisher: FEPORT (Federation of European Private Port Companies and Terminals)
title: Council continues examination of the Military Mobility Regulation - Brussels
key_claim: In May 2026 the Council's ad hoc Working Party on Military Mobility met on 22 May, followed by the Council Security Committee on 26 May, continuing examination of the proposed Regulation (presented by the Commission in November 2025); discussions focus on reducing administrative burdens and facilitating access to critical dual-use transport infrastructure, with ports positioned as strategic nodes of Europe's security and resilience.
notes: Tier 4 industry-body corroboration of the live legislative timeline (Council negotiation through mid-2026).
